hints: Look at what changes from $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$, which atom is replaced and which ion could supply the new group, then think about which solvent favours substitution over hydrolysis.
walkthrough:
Spot the chain extension**
You start with $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$ and make $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$. The carbon chain has grown by one carbon, and $\text{Cl}$ has been swapped for $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. That is the classic test for nucleophilic substitution by cyanide ion, $\text{CN}^-$.

Choose the correct solvent**
You need a soluble source of $\text{CN}^-$, so $\text{KCN}$ or $\text{NaCN}$. If you use aqueous conditions you would get a lot of $\text{OH}^-$ competition giving the alcohol. Using ethanol as solvent with heat pushes the cyanide substitution to give the nitrile.

hints: Draw out $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ and count the longest chain including the carbon of the $\text{CN}$ group, then recall what suffix replaces the final e of the alkane.
walkthrough:
Count all the carbons correctly**
Write X fully as $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Many students count only two carbons and say ethanenitrile, but the carbon in the $\text{CN}$ group counts as part of the parent chain. So you have $3$ carbons in total.

Apply the nitrile suffix**
For a $3$ carbon alkane the stem is propan, and the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ functional group gives the suffix nitrile. Put them together to get propanenitrile.

hints: Focus on the functional group change from $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ in X to $\text{COOH}$ in $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ with water supplied under dilute acid, what general class of bond breaking with water is this?
walkthrough:
See water adding across the nitrile**
In step 2, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$ becomes $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$. The $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ is broken and $\text{O}$ and $\text{OH}$ from water are added, with dilute acid acting as catalyst. Any reaction where water splits a bond in this way is hydrolysis, here specifically acid hydrolysis of a nitrile.

hints: Recall the general pattern when any carboxylic acid reacts with a reactive metal like $\text{Ca}$, what two types of product always form.
Think about the formula of the calcium salt formed from two propanoate ions with $\text{Ca}^{2+}$ and how to balance $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{Ca}$ to give that salt plus the gas.
walkthrough:
Identify Y and the gas**
Propanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, behaves as a typical acid with metal calcium. The $\text{H}$ of the $\text{COOH}$ group is displaced, so you get a salt, calcium propanoate $(\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO})_2\text{Ca}$, which is Y, the food additive, plus hydrogen gas, $\text{H}_2$.

Balance the equation**
Calcium is $2+$ so it needs two propanoate $1-$ ions to balance charge. That means you need $2$ moles of acid for $1$ mole of $\text{Ca}$:
$$2\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} + \text{Ca} \rightarrow (\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COO})_2\text{Ca} + \text{H}_2$$
Check atoms: $2$ acidic H atoms make one $\text{H}_2$, and everything else balances.

hints: Remember that propan-1-ol to $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ is a full oxidation that must go past the aldehyde stage, so think what acidic environment and heating technique prevents volatile intermediate escaping.
walkthrough:
Lock in conditions for full oxidation**
Propan-1-ol is a primary alcohol. With potassium dichromate(VI) you can stop at propanal by distillation, but to get all the way to propanoic acid you must keep everything in the flask. That means acidify the dichromate with dilute sulfuric acid and heat under reflux so any aldehyde formed condenses back and is oxidised further to the acid.
Final answer: dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / $\text{H}^+(\text{aq})$ and heat under reflux

hints: Sketch $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ and remember the rule that every single bond is one sigma bond, while each multiple bond contains one sigma plus one or two pi bonds.
Count first all sigma bonds from the five $\text{C-H}$, two $\text{C-C}$ and one component of $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$, then count the extra pi bonds left in the triple bond.
walkthrough:
Count sigma bonds systematically**
Draw $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$. Every bond starts with one sigma. You have $5$ $\text{C-H}$ single bonds giving $5$ sigma, plus $2$ $\text{C-C}$ single bonds giving $2$ sigma, plus the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond which contributes $1$ sigma. Total sigma $= 5 + 2 + 1 = 8$.

Count pi bonds from the triple bond**
A triple bond is made of $1$ sigma and $2$ pi bonds. There are no other double or triple bonds in the molecule, so total pi $= 2$.
